source_text: Igitur gradum conferamus, et summam quaestionis ipsius certis lineis determinemus. Cur etenim Deus, universitatis conditor, mundi totius gubernator, hominis plasmator, universarum gentium sator, legem per Moysen uni populo dedisse credatur, et non omnibus gentibus attribuisse dicatur? Nisi enim omnibus eam dedisset, nullo pacto ad eam etiam proselytos ex gentibus accessum habere permitteret: sed, ut congruit bonitati Dei et aequitati ipsius, utpote plasmatoris generis humani, omnibus gentibus eamdem legem dedit: quam certis et statutis temporibus observari praecepit, quando voluit, et per quos voluit, et sicut voluit. Namque in principio mundi, ipsi Adae et Evae legem dedit, ne de fructu arboris plantatae in medio paradisi ederent; quod si contra fecissent, morte morerentur: quae lex eis sufficeret, si esset custodita. In hac enim lege Adae data, omnia praecepta condita recognoscimus quae postea pullulaverunt data per Moysen, id est, Diliges Dominum Deum tuum de toto corde tuo, et ex tota anima tua; et, Diliges proximum tibi tanquam te; et, Non occides, non moechaberis, non furaberis, falsum testimonium non dices. Honora patrem tuum et matrem: et, Alienum non concupisces. Primordialis lex est enim data Adae et Evae in paradiso, quasi matrix omnium praeceptorum Dei. Denique, si Dominum Deum suum dilexissent, contra praeceptum ejus non fecissent: si proximum diligerent, id est semetipsos, persuasioni serpentis non credidissent; atque ita in semetipsos homicidium non commisissent, excidendo de immortalitate, faciendo contra Dei praeceptum; a furto quoque abstinuissent, si de fructu arboris clam non degustassent, nec a conspectu Domini Dei sui sub arbore delitescere gestissent: nec falsum asseveranti diabolo participes efficerentur, credendo ei quod similes Dei essent futuri: atque ita nec Deum offendissent, ut patrem, qui eos de limo terrae quasi ex utero matris figuraverat: si alienum non concupissent, de fructu illicito non gustassent. Igitur in hac generali et primordiali Dei lege, quam in arboris fructu observari Deus sanxerat, omnia praecepta legis posterioris specialiter indita fuisse cognoscimus, quae suis temporibus edita germinaverunt Ejusdem est enim postea subdocere legem, qui ante praemiserat praeceptum, quoniam et ipsius est erudire postea qui ante justos formare instituerat. Quid enim mirum, si is auget disciplinam qui instituit? si is perfecit qui coepit? Denique ante legem Moysi scriptam in tabulis lapideis legem fuisse contendo non scriptam, quae naturaliter intelligebatur, et a patribus custodiebatur. Nam unde Noe justus inventus, si non illum naturalis legis justitia praecedebat? unde Abraham amicus Dei deputatus, si non de aequitate et justitiae legis naturalis? unde Melchisedech sacerdos Dei summi nuncupatus, si non ante Leviticae legis sacerdotium Levitae fuerunt, qui sacrificia Deo offerebant? Sic enim post supra scriptos patriarchas data lex est Moysi eo tempore posteaquam ab Aegypto excesserunt, post intervallum multorum temporum et spatia Denique, post quadringentos et triginta annos Abrahae data est lex. Unde intelligimus Dei legem etiam ante Moysen, nec in Horeb tantum, aut in Sina et in cremo, sed antiquiorem primum in paradiso, post patriarchis, atque ita et Judaeis certis temporibus reformatam; ut non jam ad Moysi legem ita attendamus, quasi ad principalem legem, sed ad subsequentem, quam certo tempore Deus et gentibus exhibuit, et repromissam per prophetas in melius reformavit, et praemonuit futurum ut, sicuti certo tempore data est lex per Moysen, ita temporaliter observata et custodita credatur: nec adimamus hanc Dei potestatem, pro temporum conditione legis praecepta reformantem in hominis salutem. Denique, qui contendit et sabbatum adhuc observandum quasi salutis medelam, circumcisionem octavi diei propter mortis comminationem, doceat in praeteritum justos sabbatizasse aut circumcidisse, et sic amicos Dei effectos. Nam, si circumcisio purgat hominem, Deus Adam incircumcisum cum faceret, cur eum non circumcidit, vel posteaquam deliquit, si purgat circumcisio? Certe in paradiso constituens eum incircumcisum, colonum paradisi praefecit. Igitur, cum neque circumcisum neque sabbatizantem Deus Adam instituerit, consequenter quoque sobolem ejus Abel offerentem sibi sacrificia, incircumcisum nec sabbatizantem laudavit, accepto ferens quae offerebat in simplicitate cordis, et reprobans sacrificium fratris ejus Cain, qui non offerebat, non recte dividebat. Noe quoque incircumcisum Deus, sed et non sabbatizantem, de diluvio liberavit. Nam et Enoch justissimum non circumcisum, nec sabbatizantem, de hoc mundo transtulit; qui necdum mortem gustavit, ut aeternitatis candidatus, jam nobis ostenderet nos quoque sine legis onere Moysi, Deo posse placere. Melchisedech quoque summi Dei sacerdos incircumcisus, et non sabbatizans, ad sacerdotium Dei allectus est. Probat et Loth frater Abrahae, quod pro meritis justitiae suae sine legis observatione de Sodomitarum incendio sit liberatus.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore let us compare the step and determine the sum of the question itself with certain lines. For why is God, the founder of the universe, the governor of the whole world, the shaper of man, the sower of all nations, believed to have given the law through Moses to one people, and not to have attributed it to all nations? For if He had not given it to all, He would not have permitted access to it even to proselytes from the nations; but, as it is fitting to the goodness of God and His equity, as the shaper of the human race, He gave the same law to all nations, which He commanded to be observed at certain and established times, when He willed, and through whom He willed, and as He willed. For in the beginning of the world, He gave the law to Adam and Eve themselves, not to eat of the fruit of the tree planted in the middle of paradise; which if they had done against, they would have died by death; which law would have been sufficient for them if it had been kept. For in this law given to Adam, we recognize all the commandments founded which later sprouted through Moses, that is, You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul; and, You shall love your neighbor as yourself; and, You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness. Honor your father and your mother; and, You shall not covet what belongs to another. For the primordial law was given to Adam and Eve in paradise, as the matrix of all the commandments of God. Finally, if they had loved the Lord their God, they would not have acted against His commandment; if they had loved their neighbor, that is, themselves, they would not have believed the persuasion of the serpent; and thus they would not have committed homicide against themselves, cutting themselves off from immortality, acting against the commandment of God; they would also have abstained from theft, if they had not secretly tasted the fruit of the tree, nor hidden from the sight of the Lord their God under the tree. And they would not have become participants in the false assertion of the devil, believing him that they would be like God; and thus they would not have offended God, as their father, who had formed them from the clay of the earth as if from the womb of a mother. If they had not coveted what belonged to another, they would not have tasted the forbidden fruit. Therefore, in this general and primordial law of God, which God had sanctioned to be observed in the fruit of the tree, we recognize that all the commandments of the later law were specially implanted, which were published at their times and sprouted. For it is the same God who later teaches the law, who previously sent forth the commandment, since it is also His to instruct later those whom He had previously formed as just. What is surprising, if He increases discipline who instituted it? If He perfects who began? Finally, I contend that before the written law of Moses on stone tablets, there was a law that was not written, which was naturally understood and kept by the fathers. For whence was Noah found just, if not the justice of the natural law had preceded him? Whence was Abraham called the friend of God, if not from the equity and justice of the natural law? Whence was Melchizedek called the priest of the most high God, if not before the priesthood of Levi there were those who offered sacrifices to God? For thus the law was given to Moses at that time after they had come out of Egypt, after an interval of many times and spaces. Finally, after four hundred and thirty years, the law was given to Abraham. Whence we understand that God's law was also before Moses, and not only in Horeb, or in Sinai, or in the desert, but earlier, first in paradise, and later to the patriarchs, and thus also to the Jews, reformed at certain times; so that we do not now attend to the law of Moses as if it were the principal law, but as subsequent, which God certainly exhibited to the nations at a certain time, and promised through the prophets to reform for the better, and foretold that it would come to pass, that just as the law was given through Moses at a certain time, so it would be observed and kept temporarily; and we do not take away this power of God, reforming the commandments of the law according to the condition of the times for the salvation of man. Finally, he who contends that the Sabbath is still to be observed as a remedy for salvation, and circumcision on the eighth day because of the threat of death, let him teach that the just in the past observed the Sabbath or were circumcised, and thus became friends of God. For if circumcision purifies man, why did God not circumcise Adam when He made him, or afterwards, when he had sinned, if circumcision purifies? Certainly, God established him as uncircumcised in paradise, and made him the colonel of paradise. Therefore, since God did not institute Adam as circumcised or observing the Sabbath, it follows that He also praised his offspring Abel, who offered sacrifices to Him, uncircumcised and not observing the Sabbath, accepting what he offered in simplicity of heart, and rejecting the sacrifice of his brother Cain, who did not offer it rightly. God also freed Noah, uncircumcised and not observing the Sabbath, from the flood. For He also translated Enoch, the most just, uncircumcised and not observing the Sabbath, from this world; who, not having yet tasted death, showed us that we can also please God without the burden of the law of Moses. Melchizedek, the priest of the most high God, uncircumcised and not observing the Sabbath, was also drawn to the priesthood of God. And Lot, the brother of Abraham, proves that he was liberated from the burning of Sodom without observing the law, because of the merits of his justice.
pass_b_english: Let us now move forward and define the heart of the matter with precision. Why should anyone think that God—the Founder of the universe, the Governor of the world, the Shaper of man, the Sower of all nations—gave his law through Moses to a single people and withheld it from the rest? If he had not given it to everyone, he would never have allowed Gentile proselytes to approach it at all. But because it fits both the goodness and the equity of the One who shaped the human race, he gave the same law to every nation, ordering it to be kept at the specific times, through the specific people, and in the specific manner he chose.

At the very beginning, he gave Adam and Eve a law: do not eat from the tree planted in the middle of Paradise. Disobedience meant certain death. That one command would have been enough, had they kept it. In that law given to Adam we already recognize every commandment that later sprouted through Moses: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and all your soul. You shall love your neighbor as yourself. You shall not kill, commit adultery, steal, or bear false witness. Honor your father and mother. You shall not covet what belongs to another (Genesis 2:16-17; Exodus 20:1-17). This primordial law, given in Paradise, is the matrix of all God's commandments.

Had they loved the Lord their God, they would not have broken his command. Had they loved their neighbor—that is, themselves—they would have rejected the serpent's lie. They would not have committed suicide by cutting themselves off from immortality through disobedience. They would have avoided theft, since they would not have secretly tasted the fruit. They would not have hid from the Lord their God among the trees. They would not have become accomplices to the devil's false claim that they would become like God. They would not have offended their Father, who formed them from the clay of the earth as from a mother's womb. Had they not coveted another's property, they would never have touched the forbidden fruit.

Thus in this universal, primordial law—which God sanctioned to be observed in the fruit of the tree—we find every commandment of the later law already implanted, waiting to be published and to sprout in its appointed season. The God who later teaches the law is the same One who first sent the commandment; it belongs to him to instruct later those he first formed as righteous. Why should it surprise us that the One who instituted discipline also increases it, or that the One who began the work also perfects it?

I maintain that long before Moses received the written law on stone tablets, an unwritten law existed—naturally understood and kept by the fathers. How else was Noah found righteous, unless the justice of natural law had gone before him? How was Abraham called God's friend, except through the equity and justice of that same natural law? How was Melchizedek named priest of God Most High, unless there were already those who offered sacrifices to God before the Levitical priesthood existed? The law came to Moses only after the Exodus, after a long interval of time—four hundred and thirty years after Abraham.

From this we see that God's law did not begin with Moses, or at Horeb, Sinai, or the desert. It began earlier, first in Paradise, then with the patriarchs, and only later was it reformed for the Jews at set times. We must therefore stop treating the Law of Moses as the principal law. It is a subsequent law, which God gave to the nations at a specific moment, promised through the prophets to reform for the better, and foretold would be observed only temporarily—just as it was given at a specific time through Moses. We cannot strip God of his power to reform the law's precepts according to the condition of the times for the salvation of humanity.

Anyone who insists the Sabbath must still be kept as a remedy for salvation, and circumcision on the eighth day under threat of death (Genesis 17:10-14), must prove that the righteous of the past kept the Sabbath or were circumcised, and so became God's friends. If circumcision purifies a man, why did God not circumcise Adam when he created him, or after he sinned? God established him in Paradise as uncircumcised and appointed him its keeper. Since God did not institute Adam as circumcised or Sabbath-keeping, it follows that he also praised Abel—uncircumcised, not keeping the Sabbath—accepting his sacrifice offered in simplicity of heart, while rejecting Cain's, who did not offer rightly.

God also delivered Noah, uncircumcised and not keeping the Sabbath, from the Flood. He translated Enoch, the most righteous, uncircumcised and not keeping the Sabbath, from this world before he tasted death—showing us that we too can please God without the burden of the Mosaic law. Melchizedek, priest of God Most High, uncircumcised and not keeping the Sabbath, was drawn into the priesthood of God. And Lot, Abraham's brother, proves that a man can be rescued from the burning of Sodom without observing the law, purely on the merit of his own justice.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the theological arguments regarding natural law versus Mosaic law. Pass A preserves the clause structure and nuances of the Latin (e.g., 'matrix omnium praeceptorum Dei' as 'matrix of all God's commandments'). Pass B provides a fluent English rendering that maintains the agency and modality of the original (e.g., 'We cannot strip God of his power' for 'nec adimamus hanc Dei potestatem'). Scripture citations in Pass B (Genesis 2:16-17, Exodus 20:1-17, Genesis 17:10-14) correctly identify the biblical allusions in the Latin text. The title 'God's Law for All Nations' accurately reflects the central thought of the chapter.

source: 'Igitur gradum conferamus, et summam quaestionis ipsius certis lineis determinemus.', English: 'Therefore let us compare the step and determine the sum of the question itself with certain lines.'
